statement.p: Solve the inequality 12\leq4p\text{.} Graph the solution set on a number line. State the solution set using interval notation and using set-builder notation.

solution.p: Using interval notation, we write the solution set as [3, \infty)\text{.} Using set-builder notation, we write it as \{p \mid p \geq 3\}\text{.}

We should check that some number less than 3 is not a solution, that 3 itself is a solution, and that some number greater than 3 is a solution. \begin{aligned} \amp\amp 12\amp\leq4p\amp\amp\\ 12\amp\wonder{\leq}4(\substitute{0})\amp 12\amp\wonder{\leq}4(\substitute{3})\amp 12\amp\wonder{\leq}4(\substitute{5})\\ 12\amp\reject{\leq}0\amp12\amp\confirm{\leq}12\amp12\amp\confirm{\leq}20 \end{aligned} Everything worked out as expected, so our solution is reasonably checked.

BEGIN_PGML_SOLUTION To solve this inequality, we divided each side by [`4\text{.}`]
[``` \begin{aligned} 12\amp\leq4p\\ \divideunder{12}{4}\amp\leq\divideunder{4p}{4}\\ 3\amp\leq p \end{aligned} ```]
The last line says that "[`3`] is less than or equal to [`p`]". It may feel more natural to say the same thing but in the opposite order with the opposite comparison: "[`p`] is greater than or equal to [`3`]". So you could write
[``` p\geq 3 ```]
Graphically, we represent this solution set as:
>> [@image(insertGraph($image_1), width=>600)@]* <<
Using interval notation, we write the solution set as [`[3, \infty)\text{.}`] Using set-builder notation, we write it as [`\{p \mid p \geq 3\}\text{.}`]
We should check that some number less than [`3`] is _not_ a solution, that [`3`] itself _is_ a solution, and that some number greater than [`3`] _is_ a solution.
[``` \begin{aligned} \amp\amp 12\amp\leq4p\amp\amp\\ 12\amp\wonder{\leq}4(\substitute{0})\amp 12\amp\wonder{\leq}4(\substitute{3})\amp 12\amp\wonder{\leq}4(\substitute{5})\\ 12\amp\reject{\leq}0\amp12\amp\confirm{\leq}12\amp12\amp\confirm{\leq}20 \end{aligned} ```]
Everything worked out as expected, so our solution is reasonably checked.
END_PGML_SOLUTION
